newsitem.title: USA: Atlanta mayor offers $10,000 bomb reward.
newsitem.headline: Atlanta mayor offers $10,000 bomb reward.

text.p: Mayor Bill Campbell offered a $10,000 reward on Wednesday for information leading to the arrest and conviction of those responsible for the bombing of a gay and lesbian night club.

As scores of FBI and other law enforcement agents shifted their investigation to interviews with local explosives distributors, Campbell told a news conference that the bombing and a January attack on an Atlanta abortion clinic had shaken the normal tranquility of city life.
In each incident a second explosive device was left near the bomb site to explode after investigators, rescue workers and members of the media had arrived.
"The federal authorities have not seen this baited bomb ambush strategy in many years," the mayor said.
"It is in our best interest for someone to come forward with information that will allow us to capture this person that has destroyed the tranquility of our life in a city known for its tolerance."

The reward money came from the mayor's campaign funds and other sources. The nightclub bomb exploded on Friday night at the Otherside Lounge, injuring five people, including a young woman who needed surgery to remove shrapnel from her shoulder.
Georgia fire chiefs already have offered a $15,000 reward for information on the mid-January abortion clinic bombing, which injured more than half a dozen, including firefighters.

In December, the FBI announced a reward of up to $500,000 for information leading to the arrest of the July bombing at Centennial Olympic Park. That explosion left two people dead and more than 100 injured.
There have been no arrests in any of the three bombing incidents.

Members of the Atlanta gay community said they would donate money to defray losses among businesses which were forced to close for four days as investigators conducted a painstaking examination of the crime scene. The area reopened to the public on Tuesday.

A task force of 50 federal, state and local officers has begun interviewing employees of explosives distributors in the Atlanta area and examining company records, even though crime lab reports have not been completed.
"That's a routine step in any bombing case," FBI spokesman Jay Spadafore said.

"We've moved into what is normally referred to as an investigative stage, where we're interviewing witnesses and tracking down leads. Even before we assemble the device, we know what it's made out of and so we start running down the components, trying to determine where they were purchased and manufactured."
Investigators were still examining a letter claiming responsibility for both the nightclub and abortion clinic bombings on behalf of a militant Christian group called the Army of God.
